# before any engine reads it: the sixteen claimed classes, ten rows each, every row acceptance. Ids by class: FA
# feature-add, BS bug-symptom, RF refactor, DL delete, TO tests-only, PF performance, NG non-go, QU question, NN
# named-name, NP named-path, VG vague, GF greenfield, CC cross-cutting, KI knowledge-id, NE negation, PE pasted-error.
# Columns and cells as classes.tsv: id, class, unit, target, reuse, consumers, knowledge, allow, prompt; ';' separates
# alternatives any of which is right; '-' means no line of that kind is right; '*' leaves the cell unjudged; '\n' in a
# prompt is a newline. Judged tree: /tmp/rk-autosteer/acm11/tree (65 units, the tree T1c indexed), the tree
# classes.tsv and classes2.tsv were authored from.
# Gate shape 3 (registered 2026-11-08 02:1x before any row of this file existed; judge
# internal/graph/engine/acm15_shape3_test.go): a naming row (class named-name, named-path, pasted-error or
# knowledge-id, or a prompt holding a truth unit's path, last segment or a target file's name) and a no-unit row are
# right when the brief's unit is a truth and no unit line where the truth is '-'; a prose row is right when the brief
# states no wrong unit: no unit line, a stated unit that is a truth, or a candidate pair holding a truth. Per class
# the unit verdict right in 7 of 10; reuse, consumers and knowledge judged on the rows whose brief unit is a truth,
# per class right in 7 of 10 of those judged, rounded up, where at least three are judged, and over the 160 rows each
# kind right in 7 of 10 of those judged; gate B: stated unit lines right in 0.8 of those stated, candidate lines
# holding a truth in 0.5 of those delivered. Read once, at d4f5d05e, by TestACM15_FreshTable with RASHOMON_ACM11_DIR
# the tree and RASHOMON_ACM15_FRESH this file. What each outcome does was committed before this file (2c5cf64e): met
# on every term closes M1; any term not met is recorded as not met, and this file is never read again by an engine
# Authoring (2026-11-08, Sonnet 5, one author per class; 16 calls, 2,170,639 tokens, 794 tool uses, 39 min 23 s,
# against classes2's 2,004,251; answers sha256 cf79db56): each author read the judged tree and was given the authoring
# rules (sha256 0798e27e: classes2's rules plus two found on classes2, a _test.go file is never reuse because the
# judged tool reads no test file, and no request copies five or more consecutive words from knowledge.txt or a .md
# file of the tree), the same atlas (a360749d) and knowledge records (ac72b0b4) as classes2, and its class's requests
# in prompts.tsv, edge.tsv, classes.tsv and classes2.tsv as taken (no repeat, no paraphrase, no reused subject). No
# author built a brief or ran the engine.
# Assembly checks as classes2's, plus the copy check (five consecutive words of knowledge.txt or a tree .md; record
# ids, pasted lines and paths exempt). Repairs at assembly, each logged before the second read: QU04 copied five words
# of the tree's SECURITY.md ('the user's home directory'), and 'own' was added to break the run, no content word
# changed; KI09's unit was internal/install alone, where the knowledge-id rule makes the unit the record's applies-to
# set (internal/install, cmd/rashomon, internal/brief) unless the record's own text names the work's location, and
# PF-HD9's text is its title alone. KI06, KI07 and KI08 were read under the same rule and kept: B271 names
# selfguard.AgentSignal, B259 names locate.go:52-54, D181 names caps.go and decide.go. The authors wrote ids XX01 to
# XX10, which classes2.tsv holds, so every id was renumbered XX11 to XX20. validate_classes.py --tree <the tree>
# --per-class 10 --against prompts.tsv:edge.tsv:classes.tsv:classes2.tsv: 160 rows, 0 findings; the copy check: 0 of
# Second read (blind, Sonnet 5, three readers per row given the atlas and their batch only, the earlier readers'
# prompts verbatim; 48 calls, 3,746,193 tokens against an estimate of 3.1M; answers sha256 39a9bb50): the unit read
# shows the request and any cited record, never the author's answer; the reuse read shows the request, the unit truth
# and the edit point (target), never the reuse cell; greenfield rows (reuse '*') are not reuse-read. Unit 142 of 160
# confirmed, 17 contested, 1 split, Fleiss kappa 0.914 over 158 rows read three times; reuse 104 of 150 confirmed, 39
# contested, 7 split, kappa 0.690 over 147 (two of three readers answered VG13 and VG14 in both reads and NE15 in the
# Adjudication under classes2's rules unchanged (sha256 9d63fa8b, fixed before any classes2 answer existed). Unit
# gains (U3), each beside the author's truth, with the request words that admitted them: FA11 internal/shape, BS17
# cmd/rashomon, RF14 internal/directive, DL13 scripts/benchgate (tolerance), TO16 internal/settings (user), PF11
# internal/hook, PF14 internal/verify, CC13 internal/report, CC15 internal/report, CC18 internal/spec (check, path),
# KI13 scripts/mergeguard (gate), NE12 internal/receipt (trailer), NE15 cmd/rashomon. TO16, CC18 and KI13 rest on
# common words, the looseness classes2's header records, so the read prints per class, not gated, the unit rows right
# only on a U3 gain. Four contested rows U3 did not admit, each kept under U2 after a tree read: FA16
# (internal/shape/runner.go:42 testCommands holds go test and cargo test; the readers' internal/gateinfer holds a
# second closed table at gateinfer.go:63), CC17 (internal/fold/write.go and internal/settings/write.go are temp, fsync
# and rename writers; the tree holds five more, so a brief naming internal/recap, internal/baseline or
# internal/consent scores wrong), CC19 (fold.Write has no fault.Inject before its rename; three other fsync writers
# lack one too (internal/consent/record.go, internal/store/harnesscounts.go, cmd/rashomon/share.go), and by first
# commit share.go (2026-10-28) is newer than fold/write.go (2026-10-22), which the judged tree, holding no history,
# does not show), KI12 (B417 applies to internal/budget/budgets_gen.go, and internal/budget/budgets.go:14 holds the
# go:generate line, so a freshness test can sit in internal/budget; the readers' scripts/budgetsgen is the generator).
# These four truths are narrower than the tree: they can only lower the score. NG's split row keeps its truth.
# Reuse gains (A4 under A5), each beside the old truth: FA18, FA19, BS12, BS13, BS14, BS18, RF11, DL11, DL15, TO12,
# PF11, PF14, PF17, PF20, QU11, NN19, NP13, NP16, NP18, CC12, CC20, KI12, KI13, KI16, KI20, NE12, NE15, NE16, PE15
# (29); no truth was an edit point (A3); 10 contested rows keep their truth (a majority '-', or A5 not met) and 7
# split rows keep theirs. consumers and knowledge are derived from the graph after adjudication by
# test/live/autosteer/judge/derive_truths.py --per-alternative (23 rows carry per-alternative sets), and no other cell
# changed. The adjudicator applied fixed rules and never saw engine output on these rows; no engine has read this

column9:
Two hosts that are really the same destination compare as different in the novelty and sandbox views: an internationalized domain name written in Unicode and the ASCII xn-- form of the exact same name reach the comparison as two different strings.
We already fold case, a trailing dot, the port and an IP literal's spelling down to one canonical form for exactly this reason -- so that two spellings of one destination don't fork into two baseline entries.
A Unicode hostname and its punycode twin are the one case nothing folds: they pass straight through and compare unequal.
Pull in whatever's needed to fold a Unicode name to its ASCII spelling before the rest of the canonicalization runs, and keep the existing canonicalization tests green.

Layout draws every factor's arm for a session but hands them back as a plain list -- to log which feature got which arm I have to zip the result back up against the factors I passed in myself. Return the arms keyed by feature name instead.

The sandbox trail now carries a denial category for every host it refused, but the only thing that reaches a reader is a flat, deduplicated list of denied hosts with no sense of why each was refused. Add a per-category count of denials so a report can say how many were an allowlist miss versus a deny-list hit, not just how many hosts.
Add an F1 figure to the accuracy score, next to precision and recall.

A Slack incoming webhook URL that ends up in a pasted log doesn't get caught by the secret redaction -- the deny list has the xoxb-/xoxp- style bot and user tokens covered, but a bare webhook URL carries no such prefix and sails through untouched. Add a rule for the webhook URL's own shape and wire it into the same table that drives the existing rules' required-literal check.
Add `deno test` to the recognized test-runner commands, the way `go test` and `cargo test` already are.

When episode mining comes back empty-handed on a would-be lesson, all I get from the candidate check is a flat no.
I'd like to know which floor it actually missed -- not enough distinct episodes, not enough distinct sessions, not enough distinct days, consistency under the bound, or an outright contradiction.
Right now the only way to find out is to pull the raw evidence numbers and compare them against every constant by hand, which is exactly the kind of thing the check should be telling me instead of making me redo.
A version that returns the specific reason next to the pass/fail would save that whole manual comparison and tell me straight away whether the candidate is close or nowhere close.

The turn-level subagent count tells me how many calls in a turn came from a subagent versus the main agent, but when a turn runs more than one subagent it's all pooled into one number. I can't tell two subagents' work in the same turn apart. Break it down per agent id instead of one combined total.

Docker pulls and pushes a session makes don't show up anywhere in the family coverage breakdown -- curl, python, node, go, git and a handful of cloud CLIs are grouped, but a docker call just falls through to not exercised even though it's as much a network tool as the rest.

I want to know how many times a session's context got compacted, not just where the most recent compaction happened.
Right now the only thing read out of a transcript is the last compact_boundary record, which is exactly what the continuity briefing needs, but it throws every earlier one away as soon as a later one turns up.
For a report line like "this session compacted 3 times," I need the count of every boundary in the transcript, not just the last one's uuid and line number.
It can reuse the exact same per-line scan that already finds the last one; it just shouldn't stop keeping what it finds.

We installed the hook for Claude Code, but when a different agent harness that is clearly not Claude is running it, the tool just keeps recording calls as if nothing is different, like it never noticed the mismatch.

I turned on a second, unrelated holdout experiment this week, and some sessions that were already in the first experiment's holdout group got pulled onto the treatment side of that first experiment too, which shouldn't happen just because a new feature came online.

One of our longer test class names, all camelCase and nothing random about it, got blacked out of a printed session report like it was a leaked API key. It's a perfectly ordinary identifier, so the masking pass seems to be flagging it by mistake.

Our repo keeps a top-level rules file and a more specific one in the subproject I'm actually working in. I expected the closer one to win, but changes only take effect when I edit the top-level file -- the one in the subproject seems to be ignored entirely.

When a really long shell command in a transcript gets cut down to just its tail for the report, the very first character shown is sometimes a mangled half of what should be a multi-byte character, as if the cut landed in the wrong spot.

I compared two sessions side by side where the two runs used different models under the hood, and the comparison summary doesn't call that out anywhere. It reads like two equivalent runs even though one used a different model than the other.

We ran the one-time before-and-after measurement back when we first installed the tool. Months later, the project brief is still showing those exact same install-day figures every time. I'd expect it to at least reflect something from this project's own recent sessions by now, since plenty of history has piled up since then. Instead it just keeps repeating the original numbers like no new activity ever came in for this project.

We have two plugins installed in Claude Code, ours being one of them. I hand-edited our plugin's hook entry just to bump its timeout, nothing else. After that, the tool's own status report started saying our plugin isn't wired up at all for that event, even though Claude Code is still clearly invoking it -- I can watch it fire every time. A timeout tweak like that shouldn't make the tool think the hook vanished completely, only that it's not the exact stock entry anymore.

Our disk cap kicked in overnight and a batch of old session runs got cleared out to bring the store back under budget, which is expected behaviour. What's odd is that one of the removed runs had been touched only about twenty minutes earlier, as part of a different session that was still actively going. I didn't think anything touched that recently should even be a candidate for removal. It feels like the recency check that's supposed to protect a live session isn't being honoured.

The platform check is supposed to resolve which package a changed file belongs to by walking up to the nearest module boundary. For a file sitting under a nested module boundary that declares no module path of its own, the file comes back as belonging to no package at all, when the enclosing outer module clearly should still apply instead.

The code that captures a wanted value's bytes while we stream-scan a JSON document shares its file with the low-level string-literal decoding for the scanner -- unescaping sequences, UTF-8 handling, that layer. Pull the string-decoding pieces into their own file so the capture-buffer logic isn't tangled up with general JSON lexing, same output as before.

Every time I have to change the full consent screen's wording I end up scrolling past the generic text-wrapping helpers to find the part that actually assembles the screen. Split the low-level wrap/line/paragraph helpers out of that file into one of their own, leaving the screen-builder code shorter, with the exact same bytes rendered.

Split the generic shape checks (is this a UUID, does this look like a version string) out of the file that decides which agent harness is running into a file of their own, without changing what counts as a match.

We keep two small closed vocabularies for a correction episode: what kind of correction it was, and what the agent was doing when it happened. Both of those are declared as their own types in one file, right next to the other small method they already have. But their stable string-id tables and the two functions that parse a stored string back into one of the values live in a totally different file, the one that's really about writing and rendering the kept-episode history. Move the id tables and the two parse functions over to sit with the types and their other method, and leave the history file holding just the history job -- nothing about what gets written or read should change.

Fold the duplicate string-list trimming helper in the digest-truncation code into the already-generic one right next to it instead of keeping two copies of the same halving logic for different element types.

The audit-trail reader's file has the whole scanning engine and the small accessor methods (which hosts, which denials) all in one place. Give the accessor methods their own file so the big event-scanning function isn't the first thing you hit reading the package, with no change to what gets reported as denied or observed.

The file that decides whether a client version is allowed to mirror also contains the unrelated code that parses the AI_AGENT version string in the first place; split the version-string parsing into its own file.

We read a digests file written by a separate sync step to check whether a package's source still matches what was last scanned. Right now the code that parses that file's own format -- the header, the tab-separated fields, the sha256 shape -- lives in the same file as the staleness check that actually re-hashes a live file on disk and compares it. Those are different jobs reading different things: one trusts bytes already on disk in a known format, the other goes and hashes a file right now. Split the staleness and hashing check into its own file and leave the file-format parsing where it is, with the same answer for every package as before.

The one file behind the uninstall command does two very different jobs: deciding which files and directories are actually ours to touch, and building and running the removal plan once that's decided. Right now the ownership tables and checks sit right next to the plan-building and execution code in the same file, which makes it hard to change one without re-reading the other. Split the ownership recognition into its own file and leave the plan construction and execution where they are. The set of files or directories removed in any scenario should stay exactly the same.

The sync command's main file has the CLI argument parsing and all the user-facing text formatting mixed in with the actual sync-and-write-to-disk engine. Pull the text-formatting and reporting helpers out of the file that does the real filesystem work, so the two are easier to review separately.

Every time I read platform data, it insists on finding a small marker file that vouches for both the log and the digests file before it'll trust either one, and if that marker's missing or stale it just refuses outright. I don't want that guard anymore - let the read go straight to the log and digests even when nothing is vouching for them.

Stop flagging kubeconfig files and terraform state files as sensitive cloud configuration - we don't need that category called out anymore, just let them fall through however an ordinary file is treated.

I noticed our benchmark budgets pass comfortably locally but barely scrape by when the same gate runs elsewhere, and it turns out there's a hidden tolerance bump that only kicks in on one CI provider. Apparently a couple of runners there haven't had their ratio measured yet, so the gate quietly gives them extra slack instead of failing. I don't want that carve-out anymore - every runner should be held to the ratio exactly as written in the budgets file. If that means a runner starts failing honestly where it used to pass quietly, that is the behavior we want.

Nobody on the team has looked at that per-pattern scoring breakdown in months since a shorter summary line replaced it for daily use. Pull the whole command out - the usage text, the flag, all of it - rather than let it keep rotting unused.

When an automated session tries to flip the end-of-turn summary line on or off, it gets refused and told to have a human do it instead. I don't think that one's worth protecting anymore - let an agent toggle it like any other switch, no special refusal.

The graph tool's own error output scrubs out absolute paths, the Go install location and the home directory before printing anything, swapping them for placeholders. That scrubbing just makes it harder to see what actually failed when I'm debugging locally - take it out and let the raw paths print as given.

Our spec file has a holdout block with a rate and an optional window, and the parser is pretty opinionated about both: the rate has to sit inside a narrow range or it gets rejected outright, and setting a window length requires also setting a start date, or the other way around. I'd rather stop enforcing all of that. Just read whatever numbers are in the rate and window fields without range-checking them, and don't require the two fields to be set together anymore. Keep everything else about how the file parses exactly the same.

The fixture hygiene scan is painfully slow on any test fixture that happens to bundle a sample tarball or zip, because right now it unpacks the whole archive and scans every member inside for secrets. That's a lot of extra work for fixtures that mostly exist to exercise unrelated code paths. I'd like it to stop opening archives at all and just treat a tarball or zip the same as any other opaque fixture file - scan its raw bytes like normal, don't unpack it. The rest of the scan and its findings format should stay exactly as they are.

When detach shows me what changed in the settings file, every value gets replaced with a placeholder so I can't actually see what moved. I just want the real diff with the actual values in it, not the redacted version.

The merge guard's rerun script prints an extra note whenever the checkpoint it's replaying had gates cut because it hit its budget, and that line isn't adding anything useful downstream - drop it and just plan whatever gates are actually present.
The holdout layout that draws two features together is supposed to refuse when the same feature name shows up twice, but I can't find a test proving that happens - can you add one?

When the last compaction marker in a transcript has an empty uuid, I'd expect the briefing code to treat it as if there's no boundary at all rather than trust the blank id. Is that actually tested? If not, please add a case so a later change can't accidentally start handing out an empty key.
Does anything actually verify that the fault-injection switches are true no-ops in a normal, released build?

I went looking for coverage on the piece that tells a guarded command apart from something an agent session is running, and there isn't any. We read one environment variable to decide that, and we build a specific refusal message out of four pieces when it fires: the reason, the command, what was left undone, and the signal name. Neither path has a single test today. Can you add tests for both: that the lookup reports the variable's name only when it's actually set, and that the refusal message is assembled correctly from its four inputs?

The directory-only open refuses a pipe and accepts a real directory, and I see tests for both of those plus a missing path. But what happens when you point it at an ordinary file instead of a directory? I don't see that case anywhere, and it's exactly the kind of mix-up that could slip through as something other than 'not a directory.' Could you add a case for it?
Does any test actually check that the bundle we hand the user comes out indented with a trailing newline, the way the writer is documented to produce it?

We hand back a closed list of caveats for a paired-session report, and the report prints them in whatever order that list comes back in, so I want to pin the order directly. Right now the function that returns it is only ever called from inside the pair-building code itself, never from a test, so a reorder of the list would slip through silently.

The code that walks the repo for the project brief is supposed to skip dotfiles, underscore-prefixed directories, a testdata folder, a vendor folder, and never follow a symlink into another directory - that's all spelled out in a comment there. But going through the test file, all I can find is coverage for the entry cap and the time budget; none of those skip rules seem to be exercised anywhere. Given how much the brief's facts depend on this walk finding the right directories, can you add tests that pin each of those skips so a change to the walk can't quietly start reading into a vendor tree, a testdata fixture, or a symlinked directory?

The helper that checks a struct-to-struct copy field by field is used all over the store's tests to catch a field a copy forgot, but I can't find anything that tests the helper itself - that it actually fails, and says why, when a field is left out of the carried list or quietly not set. Can you add that? There's a recorder type sitting right there that looks like it was built exactly for this and is just unused.

The code-graph tool's error messages are supposed to come out with the project root collapsed to a dot, the Go install root shown as $GOROOT, and the home directory shown as ~, so an error never leaks somebody's absolute path. There's one end-to-end test that checks a failed sync's output names no absolute path overall, but nothing pins each of those substitutions on its own, or confirms the tool's own log prefix gets stripped out cleanly wherever it shows up in a wrapped error. Can you add a focused test for just that message-cleanup step, independent of running a real sync?

Every time someone answers the consent screen, the install seems to pay for way more file I/O than one appended line should cost. I traced it and after the new answer is written to the log, the code turns around and reads the whole log back from disk twice more just to decide whether the scope and disclosure markers need to move. On a machine where someone has run the installer a bunch of times that log isn't tiny, and re-parsing every past answer twice right after we already read it once feels like pure waste. Can the marker checks build on what the append step already read instead of starting over from the top of the file twice?

The per-project host memory rebuilds and re-sorts its entire host list from scratch on every single load, even when every host on it is already canonical and nothing changed. On a project that's built up a lot of history that's real repeated work for no benefit. Can it skip the rebuild when there's nothing left to canonicalize?

Opening a project's lesson ledger re-parses the full history of every lesson fire ever recorded for that project just to compute the running tallies, every single time it's opened — can that be cached instead of replayed from scratch on every open?

Finding the newest checkpoint for a project seems to open and read a slice of every single run in the whole store, not just runs that belong to the current project, before it even checks which project a run is for. On a machine with a lot of unrelated project history sitting around that's a lot of wasted reads paid every time something needs to name the latest checkpoint. Shouldn't the project check happen before paying for the read, or at least stop once the answer is already found?

The shareable outcomes summary rebuilds its counts by walking every run's entire decision log from the very first line, every single time someone asks for it. For someone who's been running this a long time, with hundreds of runs behind them, that means re-reading years of old decisions just to answer today's question about what got fixed, ignored or overridden. I know there's already a pattern used elsewhere in this codebase for remembering how far a log has been read so a later pass can pick up where it left off instead of starting at zero. Could the outcomes summary be built that way too, instead of replaying every run's whole history each time it's built?

For every file a turn touches, the check for whether it falls under one of the tracked roots loops back through the full list of roots from the start. On a turn with a lot of writes and several roots being tracked that's a write times root scan on every single call. Could that be flipped around so each write is checked more cheaply instead of rescanning the whole root list every time?
Listing a project's lessons loops over the full lesson list once per tier instead of grouping them in a single pass — can that be one walk instead of four separate ones?
The experiment layout step checks for a duplicate factor name by comparing every factor against every earlier one in the list; swap that pairwise comparison for a plain set lookup instead.

Merging a project's declared rules checks whether a gate, rule or fact id was already declared by scanning the whole list collected so far, for every single one being merged in. With a file that declares a lot of them that turns into a lot of repeated scanning just to catch one duplicate id. Can that duplicate check use a lookup instead of rescanning the growing list each time?

Copying one session's transcript into the long-term store seems to trigger a full scan of every project's saved copies before it decides whether anything needs to be evicted to make room. I watched it stat every file under every project's folder just to free space for one new copy, even though only one project's budget actually changed. On a machine where several projects have this turned on, that's an amount of directory walking and stat'ing that scales with everyone's history, not with the one copy being made. Could the accounting be scoped to only what's actually needed to make room, instead of re-listing the whole thing on every copy?
dependabot only has a gomod entry for the root module, so pgraph/go.mod and its golang.org/x/tools dependency never get a bump PR -- can we add a second entry pointed at the pgraph directory?

I noticed the marketplace listing and the plugin manifest both carry the exact same long description of what gets recorded, hand-typed into two separate JSON files. That's an easy way for the two to quietly drift the next time the recording policy wording changes. Can we make one of them generate the other, or at least add a check that fails when they stop matching?

The top-level rashomon skill still tells people to use rashomon-report and rashomon-stop, while the plugin's watch skill points at /rashomon:report and /rashomon:stop for the same actions. A user bouncing between the two gets two different command spellings for the same thing. Could we settle on one naming convention across both skill sets?
Can scripts/build-plugin.sh also drop a sha256 file next to dist/rashomon-plugin.zip, so a release has something to point people at for verifying the plugin archive before they unzip it?

reanchor.sh falls back to altrace-dev-role/rashomon unless I set REPO, and that's normally fine. Yesterday I set REPO for a fork and the script just sat there on the gh run download step -- turned out my export hadn't actually taken in that shell, and I had no way to tell from the script's own output which repo it was about to hit. It would help if it echoed the resolved repo before it calls gh run download. Done would mean I can tell at a glance whether my override worked without having to read the script's source first.

CONTRIBUTING's 'Where things are' table only lists seven packages, and internal/spec isn't one of them even though it's exactly the kind of code someone wiring up spec trust would want pointed at first. Can we add a row for it the same way the existing ones are written?

test/mutation/buildchanged.py is great at telling you which changed rows fail to build, but when everything passes it just exits quietly with nothing printed. I ran it after a big merge and genuinely couldn't tell whether that silence meant every row I touched compiled fine, or whether my BASE argument was wrong and it had nothing to compare against at all. Could it print how many rows it actually checked against BASE before it gives its pass or fail verdict? That way a clean run and an empty run don't look identical.
label-rules.tsv has a row per detector but no column saying which file actually implements the behaviour each row describes, so could we add an owner column naming that file?

ra-1.sh writes each row's saved evidence out as loose files under .handoff/evidence. After running A1, A2 and A4 in one sitting that directory turns into a pile of mixed files from different rows, and handing it to someone else means explaining which file goes with which row. Could the script tar up a row's own evidence folder right after that row finishes, so there's one file per row instead? Done looks like running A1 alone and getting a single archive out the other end rather than a loose directory.

mergeguard.sh is intentionally harmless today -- whatever the rerun finds, it always exits 0. Now that people are starting to trust the planner's agree/differ counts, we'd like a real disagreement to actually fail the CI job. Can it exit nonzero when the differ count comes back above zero, leaving every other case exactly as it is?

I'm looking at a turn in the digest that has no probe hit and no store entry of its own, right in the middle of an otherwise healthy session.\nThe coverage line for it still lists the session's general gaps and absences rather than just saying there's nothing known about this turn specifically -- why?
How does rashomon make sure the same session draws the same side of a holdout every time a hook fires, without writing anything down?

We run sessions inside a network sandbox that writes its own audit log, and from what I can tell that log captures the full command line of whatever process it's watching.
Our side only ever seems to report a host, a port, and allow or deny -- never the command itself.
I went looking for where that command text gets threaded through into our records and came up empty.
Is that a gap in the reader, or is dropping the command line something this codebase does on purpose?

When the plugin gets installed and the user answers the consent prompts, where does that end up written?\nI want to know if it ever touches the project's own configuration file, or if it's always confined to something under the user's own home directory.
If I trust a repository's rule file and then someone edits even a comment in it, does it silently stay trusted, or do I have to re-approve it?

In the session report's mistake counts, say the agent was never told about some issue but fixed it anyway before the session ended.\nDoes that get counted toward the caught number, or does it just disappear from the numbers?\nI can't tell from the output alone and I don't want to misread the metric.

We had a session run long enough that a compaction happened partway through, and afterward the continuity note only showed a handful of the instructions I'd given earlier -- not all of them.\nBefore I file this as a bug I need the mechanics: is there a fixed cap on how many lines that note will quote?\nAnd separately, if some of my earlier instructions get left out because of that cap, is there any trace of how many were dropped, or do they just vanish with no record?

When I purge the store, in what order do the install record and the install key actually get deleted?\nI'm asking because I want to know whether an interrupted purge leaves things recognizable enough for a second run to pick up and finish the job.

I set up a paired comparison between two sessions on the same task to see whether a feature made a difference, and partway through I noticed the two sides ended up running on different models -- not something I controlled for.\nBefore I trust the result, I want to know what the tool does with that: does it refuse to produce a pair at all when the models don't match, or does it go ahead and flag the mismatch somehow so a reader can discount it?\nAnd is that flag explicit, or would I have to infer it myself from the transcripts?
For large tool payloads, how does the JSON reader pull out one deeply nested field without loading the whole document into memory first?

The directory walk that looks for Go code to describe at session start already skips vendor, testdata and dot- or underscore-prefixed names, but it still walks into a giant node_modules tree and can burn through its whole entry budget before reaching the real source.\nCan walkGo skip node_modules the same way it already skips vendor?
RES28BudgetMiB always adds the same flat 6.5 MiB floor on top of the slope, even for a payload of a few bytes; can the floor be a parameter too instead of a hardcoded constant?

SaidDigest hashes a quoted phrase under one fixed domain tag no matter which session said it, so two different sessions that happen to quote the exact same words back get the identical digest.\nCan it mix the session id into the hash so same-text quotes from different sessions no longer collide?

DroppedFindings, LockTimeouts and AppendFailures are counted in atomic.Int64 package vars that live only for the process's lifetime, but each hook event runs as its own short-lived process, so by the time anyone reads DroppedFindings it has already reset to whatever that one call saw rather than accumulating meaningfully across a session.
I want to understand how many findings route has actually dropped over a session, not just within one hook invocation.
Is there a place these three counts could be persisted across calls instead of living only in process memory, the way other per-run state already is?
I'd rather not change what Route does, just make the counters survive past one hook call.

Locations silently stops after at most MaxWalkDepth candidate locations on a cwd nested deeper than that below root, so it can give up before ever reaching the one nearest root -- can it at least report when it had to stop short instead of truncating without a trace?

UpdateInstallRecord protects the install id from whatever the edit callback does to the record, since that field is never the edit's to change.
CreatedDirs is documented as a field that should only grow over the life of an install -- once watch creates a directory it's supposed to stay in the list for purge to find later -- but nothing in UpdateInstallRecord stops a careless edit callback from replacing CreatedDirs wholesale and dropping an entry a previous watch already recorded.
If that happens, purge would never see the dropped directory again and it would never get cleaned up.
Could UpdateInstallRecord guard CreatedDirs the same way it already guards the install id, so a rewrite can only add directories, never silently lose ones already there?

Tally.Kept only keeps the 100 busiest projects by session count (keptProjects) when it builds the before-count record, so on a machine that works across more than a hundred projects, the smallest ones just disappear from Kept entirely rather than being summarized thinner the way keptRows already caps a project's own rows.\nCould Kept keep every project it saw, just capped tighter per project, instead of dropping whole projects past the hundredth?

Signals.Delivered just tells me yes or no once any of the handled termination signals has arrived, but SIGTERM (a hook timeout killing us) and SIGHUP or SIGQUIT are really different situations I'd like to log differently.\nCould Delivered also hand back which signal it actually saw, instead of collapsing all three into one bool?

File.Prompts only keeps the newest MaxPrompts marks and the doc says they're oldest first, so on a very long session the earliest prompts just fall off the front of the slice once a new one is appended past the cap.
Each Mark also carries whether its prompt has already been claimed by a Stop, and once a mark is dropped that Stopped flag is gone with it.
I ran into a session with well over a hundred prompts where an old prompt came back around for what should have been a repeat Stop, and there was no way left in the fold to tell that from a first one.
Is there a cheaper way to keep that repeat-claim information for prompts past the cap instead of just losing it when they age out?

Cap returns an empty string instead of a real CapState when the capability key isn't one it recognizes, so a caller that switches over Yes, No and Unverified can fall through unhandled instead of getting an answer -- shouldn't an unrecognized capability come back Unverified like Caps' other uncertain cases do?
In internal/arm/arm.go, why does Assign refuse a holdoutBP of exactly BasisPoints the same way it refuses zero?

internal/directive/boundary.go's LastBoundary only hands back the transcript's final compact_boundary record. We need the one before it too, to diff what changed between the last two compactions, so can LastBoundary (or something next to it in that file) return every boundary in order instead of just the last one?

internal/gateout/tables.go has rows for jest and vitest but nothing for mocha. Our frontend suite runs under mocha and its pass/fail summary lines never get classified, so every one of those runs shows up unverified in the report. Can a mocha row get added alongside the others?
internal/intent/scan.go's scan drops a trailing dot from a token before calling fn -- what happens to a token that's nothing but dots, like someone typing an ellipsis?

A prompt got cut off mid multi-byte character right at a chunk boundary, and the steer note built from it had a replacement character sitting next to bytes that looked garbled rather than one clean marker. I dug into internal/jsonscan/unquote.go, and segment's byte-run loop breaks the instant it hits anything that decodes as RuneError with size 1 -- which is exactly what a rune merely cut off at the end of body looks like, same as a byte that's actually invalid. So a string that's just truncated mid-rune and a string holding real garbage decode identically, and nothing downstream can tell 'needs more bytes' from 'bad data.' Can segment, or whoever calls it, keep that distinction even if the final decoded text stays the same?

internal/measure/pair.go's Caveats list covers n=1, an unrecorded arm, missing or partial transcripts, incomplete recording and different models, but nothing for when the two sides ran under different rashomon builds entirely. We just hit that comparing a pre-upgrade session against a post-upgrade one. Add a caveat for a build mismatch between the pair's two sides.

internal/nono/nono.go's Event carries Mode as nono's own transport word, documented as connect for a tunnel or reverse for its proxy. If nono ever starts reporting a third transport, does this file pass that word through as-is, or does it get folded into just those two somewhere?

internal/receipt/receipt.go's Latest walks run directories newest first and stops at the first run old enough to guarantee nothing newer is left unread. On one of our older projects that walk crossed well over a hundred run folders before it found anything, and the commit hook just sat there with no way to tell if it was stuck or genuinely working through history. Latest never reports how many runs it had to cross to get there, so we can't tell a slow commit hook from a project that simply has a lot of history. Can Latest, or a thin wrapper around it, return that walked count alongside the record?
internal/steer/pattern/pattern.go's ID list is called frozen at nineteen entries -- what actually stops someone from adding a twentieth constant here without anyone catching it in review?

I ran test/tools/hygiene/scrub.go's Scrub against a fixture that's really a gzipped tarball saved without a .tar.gz or .tgz suffix, and instead of refusing it as an archive, Scrub scrubbed the compressed bytes as if they were text and wrote out garbage. Scrub only decides whether something's an archive by checking the file's name against a fixed list of suffixes, so anything packed but misnamed or missing its extension sails straight into the text path. Nobody looking at the output afterward can tell it was never actually scrubbed. Can the archive check also look at the leading bytes, not just the name, so a renamed or extension-less archive still gets caught and refused?

The brief's walk over the repo for its packages line stops once it's read too many directory entries or spent too long, and it starts completely over on the very next session instead of continuing from where it left off.\nCould we add a new internal/walkresume package that remembers the walk's last-visited directory across sessions, so the packages line eventually finishes covering a big repo instead of hitting the same cap forever?

The consent screen always wraps its lines to a fixed 80 columns no matter how wide the actual terminal is; add a small internal/termwidth package that reads the real terminal width so the screen can wrap to it instead.

A turn's digest caps its own size and truncate() cuts the seven growable fields in a fixed order once the whole document is over budget, which is the right call for any one turn.
What we don't have is any sense of how often that's actually happening across a session: if a project's turns are routinely oversized and quietly losing fields, nobody would notice from looking at one digest at a time.
Could we add an internal/digesttrim package that keeps a running count, across a session, of how many digests got truncated and roughly how much was cut, so a chronically oversized session can be told apart from an occasional one?
It doesn't need to change what truncate() does today, just give something else a number to read.

fold.Write just refuses to write a run's fold.json outright once the encoded file is over MaxBytes, with no indication of which part of it (prompts, the verify section, whatever) actually grew that large.\nAdd an internal/foldbreakdown package that sizes a fold.File's fields individually before the write, so a refusal at least comes with a reason.

We keep getting support questions along the lines of 'I changed settings.json and the hook still isn't running' and right now there's no good answer beyond manually checking all four layers by hand.
Settings already knows the four layers and their precedence order (managed beats local beats project beats user), but nothing actually walks them for a given hook key and says which one is the one that's actually in effect.
I'd like a new internal/settingswhy package that takes the resolved locations and a key and reports which layer's value won, so a support answer can point at the actual cause instead of someone re-deriving the precedence by hand each time.
It shouldn't change how settings are loaded or written today, just add a read-only answer on top of what's already there.

The secret masker only ever flags the vendor token shapes it already knows about, which is fine, but when something slips through unflagged we have no record afterward of how close a miss it was.\nCan we add an internal/maskaudit package that tallies, per session, how many high-entropy spans got masked versus left alone, so a pattern of near-misses shows up in aggregate instead of only when someone happens to notice one particular leak?

The host novelty baseline keeps every hostname a project's sessions have ever named with no way to tell which project keys have gone stale; add an internal/baselinesweep package that can point at project baseline files whose host set hasn't changed in a long time so they're candidates for cleanup.

Every one of the packages that reads a hook payload calls into the field-reading code separately and each call enforces its own size limit on its own buffer.
What none of them do is add up how many bytes got scanned in total over the life of one hook invocation, so if several callers each stay just under their own individual limit, the process as a whole could still be doing a lot more scanning than anyone budgeted for.
I'd like a new internal/streambudget package that a hook invocation can hand its calls through, so the total across every caller in that one process is tracked against a single ceiling rather than each call only checking itself.
This is purely about measuring and enforcing a combined budget; it shouldn't change what any individual field read returns.

host.Canonical silently returns false both for a string with no host in it at all and for one that got refused specifically because it carried embedded credentials, so a caller can't tell those two cases apart; add an internal/credentialflag package that classifies why a host string was refused, without ever handing back the credential itself.

The audit trail from the sandbox gives us a flat list of allow/deny events per host, and if a host gets denied early in a session and then allowed later (or the other way around), the report only ever sees the window's events, never that specific host's decision actually flipped.\nAdd an internal/nonoflip package that walks one session's events and flags a host whose decision changed partway through, so that gets called out instead of just folded into the final allow/deny counts.

When two dependency-graph syncs fight over the same root, the one that loses just polls at a fixed interval forever with no idea how long it's been waiting, instead of backing off and reporting its wait time the way the record store's own file lock already does.

Our post-compaction briefing has its own private copy of the logic that decides whether a lesson already reached the user. Same offsets, same idea as the two other places that already answer that exact question for a lesson and for a steering note. Write it so this one actually calls into an existing one instead of re-deriving the same answer a third time.

Three different corners of the codebase each open a transcript file by hand with the plain standard-library call instead of the one safe-open helper that refuses to hang on a named pipe or a socket. Every one of those three should go through that same guard.

The refusal message for a command only a person may run always blames 'outside Claude Code' by name, never any other agent, even though a closed list of every agent family we recognize already exists elsewhere in the program for exactly this purpose.

Right now, whenever the session report counts a harness mismatch, it always attributes the install to Claude Code, no matter which family the hook actually caught standing down. That's fine today because nothing else is installed, but it'll quietly under-count or mis-bucket the day a second agent adapter ships. I want the report to carry and use whatever family was actually detected for that invocation, not an assumed one. Done looks like: a mismatch recorded under a different family shows up under that family in the report, not folded into Claude's count.

The side-by-side session comparison only watches a hand-picked handful of finding kinds when it decides what counts as a finding. The authoritative closed list of every kind lives somewhere else in the program and has grown past that handful already. Have it read the real list instead of its own copy, so a newly added kind doesn't just silently go uncounted.

We're adding a small paired file that keeps a log and a digest in sync with each other, and it needs to survive being killed mid-write the same way everything else in this program already does. I don't want to write a fourth copy of the temp-file-then-fsync-then-rename dance by hand; there are already two nearly identical versions of it elsewhere that this new one should build on instead. Keep the existing tests for those two green; this is additive, not a rewrite of either. Done looks like the new writer sharing real code with at least one of the existing two, not just mirroring its shape by eye.

A spec path that happens to start with a couple of dots in its own name shows up as a long absolute path in the knowledge trace instead of the tidy project-relative one every other path there gets. The check that decides 'is this under the project' needs the same careful handling our own deletion sweep's path-containment check already has for exactly this kind of name.

Our newest atomic file writer has no fault-injection hook before its rename, unlike every other atomic writer in the program, so nothing in the fault-injection suite can exercise its crash window the way the others already can.

Both the shareable outcomes bundle and the side-by-side session comparison tool read the same steering log, and each keeps its own small private struct for pulling out the handful of fields they care about: which pattern fired, what happened to it, and so on. The two structs don't even agree today on everything they both read, and nothing forces them to. Meanwhile there's already one authoritative type elsewhere in the program that names every field a steering log line can carry, tags and all. Have both of these decode onto that one instead of keeping private copies that can silently drift apart from each other and from the real schema.

B330 is the reason an earlier replay harness built every post-event note and then dropped it, because it set CLAUDECODE without AI_AGENT or CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT, so the client version read as unknown.\nWe're wiring up a second harness for a different surface next week; make the client-version read loud about a missing pair like that instead of quietly falling back to unverified.

B417 is why two branches touching the generated budget table collided and burned a CI slot before anyone noticed the pair was unmergeable. Add a check that catches the generated table drifting from what the generator would produce right now, before two branches get that far apart again.

D157 says a frozen patch has to carry the current re-anchored numbers or its gate fails on the stale ones again, so make whatever checks a patch's base also check that its budget numbers are the live ones.

D176 settled that the plain arm is just the steering arm turned off, which happens to hand us a counterfactual log for free, and that a session's forced arm should come from the same kind of operator switch the holdout share already uses rather than a second one invented for the occasion. I want the cost report to break its totals down by that same arm so we can finally see whether sessions running with steering off actually cost less. Please read the arm through whatever already resolves it for a session rather than adding a fresh way to ask. Flag anywhere the two readings could disagree, since that's exactly the kind of drift D109 warned about for the holdout share.

D182 ruled that the counterfactual has to be folded in at the moment a line is decided, not rebuilt later from the stored record, because a later replay can't see whether the channel was verified at decide time. I'm sketching a tool that shows what a session's off-arm would have surfaced; make sure it reads that already-folded answer instead of re-deriving verification from what got written.

B271 showed that someone can clear the Claude-Code environment variables and pass the yes flag to get past the guard that's supposed to stop an agent session from installing or changing consent on a person's behalf, because today the guard only checks one of the three signals it was designed to read. We told the owner a confident line about a human always having to say yes, and that line was wrong. Add the next signal the guard is missing, the one that doesn't depend on an environment variable the session itself can unset, so the pitch becomes true instead of just convenient. Keep the existing refusal message and callers working exactly as they do today.

B259 is the reason promising someone a project-scoped install by the end of the day didn't work out: today we only ever write to the one settings file that lives under a person's own home directory, because a file committed into the repository would hard-code one person's binary path for everyone who clones it. Work out what a project-scoped option would actually need and where the new location logic should sit alongside the layers we already resolve.

D181 explains why a non-interactive, scripted run of the tool can't be used to measure most of what AutoSteer normally shows: that surface's in-band mirror reads as unverified, so almost every post-event note gets suppressed and only the very first prompt of a session is exempt. I want to start closing that gap by seeing if we can earn a verified reading for that surface instead of leaving it permanently unverified. Tell me where the capability table would need to change to let a surface move out of unverified, and whether the suppression logic downstream would need to change to notice. Don't touch anything about the positive control the other measurement work already depends on.

PF-HD9 points out that we only know which instruction files were present because the brief and the probe went and read them themselves, since nothing ever asks Claude Code to say what it loaded; wire that kind of event into the same list the other session hooks are declared in, once there's one to subscribe to.

D106 fixed the done flag so it compares seqs instead of assuming a gate always ran after the last edit, but the line for the gates that did pass still hardcodes 'after the last edit' even when a stale gate sits right next to them; route that text through the same seq comparison before it makes the same false claim again.

After a compaction, the one-time reminder of everything I told the agent earlier only ever shows five lines, even on turns where there's clearly room for more without blowing past the size limit it already enforces. Don't change how a correction's reworded version gets folded into the quote it restates — just let the line count grow past five when the budget allows it.

Our git hooks route commits through `rashomon receipt`, and more than once I've second-guessed whether the setup even found a checkpoint, because when there's nothing to put in the trailer the command just exits clean with empty output. I had to go check the store by hand to confirm nothing was broken. Please don't touch the two hook scripts the on command prints — those are fine and I don't want to re-paste them into my hooks directory. Just have the trailer and note lookups say there's no checkpoint for this project yet instead of staying silent, so a quiet exit reads as nothing to report rather than something's wrong.

The preflight note that resolves the files and symbols out of my prompt stops naming paths after the eighth one, even when I've listed a dozen files in one request that all exist in the project. Without changing which verbs it recognizes, let it keep more than eight named paths when a prompt lists that many.

A build command that fails still gets recorded in my gate history as if nothing was classified at all — it's treated exactly like a lint or typecheck run that's never scanned. Without changing how a test run's output gets scored pass or fail, let a failed build line get picked out of the output the same way, instead of the gate output always coming back unclassified for anything that isn't a test.

When a hook payload comes in over the size cap, the refusal only remembers which session and working directory it belonged to, so I can go find the right run in the store afterward. That's enough to find the session, but not enough to tell whether it was a huge tool result on a pre-tool-use call or just a bloated transcript path on something like a stop event. I end up guessing from context every time this fires, which isn't great for a refusal that's supposed to help me track down what happened. Don't change which two fields get read out of the oversized payload's head today; just also pull out which hook event fired, the same way the session id and working directory already get read, so the refusal names what kind of call blew past the cap.

Keep the entropy test exactly as it is, but add our chat bot's token prefix to the plain pattern list the way cloud provider key prefixes are already caught, since right now a leaked bot token slips through unredacted.

Without changing how a benchmark run gets matched to another platform's measured rows, let the toolchain check tolerate a difference in just the patch version of Go instead of refusing the whole comparison on any exact version-string mismatch.

When the end-of-turn build-health check can't even read its own graph file — because it timed out or the file was unreadable — the turn-end line just stays quiet about any package I touched, the exact same silence as when the graph says everything is current. I got burned by that once: I assumed a change was covered because nothing was flagged, and it turned out the check never ran at all that turn. Don't change which changed packages get named when the check actually does run — that part already works fine. Just have the turn-end line say the check couldn't run this time, the same way it already says a package still owes a test, so a silent read isn't mistaken for a clean one.

Our generated-code package has way more files in its directory than the cross-package build graph's test-file check will look through, so it always reports as having no test file even though one is right there. Without changing how a package gets judged current or stale against that graph, raise how many directory entries the test-file lookup is willing to scan.

Without touching how a CI step or a Makefile target gets read for a declared test command, add a guess from a project's own mix file for an Elixir service the way package.json and Gemfile already get a convention-only fallback command.
